newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian wages data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian wages data.

text.p: Australian wages rose 1.2 percent in the three months to November to be 3.9 percent higher over the year, The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
The result was at the top end of economists forecasts, which had centred on a 0.9 percent rise in the quarter for an annual rate of 3.6 percent.
Annual forecasts ranged from 3.3 to 3.9 percent.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow.
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"Well it certainly is a disappointment to see the trend fall in wages broken, and if the Reserve Bank is concerned about wage rises in the future, this sort of figure doesn't help. Keep in mind that they have that line in the sand at about 4.5 percent, with the living wage case now in front of the Industrial Relations Commission, and a few other negotiations in place. If they believe wage growth (is) moving towards say five percent, it will certainly make them hesitate and certainly think twice even about an easing March."
PETER MUNCKTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"Well clearly it is a disappointment as the market had brought itself up for another fall but I think we can basically say it is broadly in line with the number we had last time. Last time it was 3.8 (percent annual), this time it is 3.9. For monetary policy, we thought going into the number that there was a less than 50-50 chance of them easing once again. This number doesn't change our view there. But if you have wages of something around four percent or a tad less, and inflation of two percent then I don't think the wages/inflation numbers are necessarily of a concern, it is the activity data."
JEFF OUGHTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"It looks like that while ordinary time earnings are about four percent on a year-ended basis, average earnings are running at about 2.5 percent. And what that means is, and particularly in the last quarter, there's been a number of larger claims go through, for example in the banking and a few other sectors. But in trend terms now wages are running at around 3.5 percent, and if you add on to that the continuance of the enterprise bargaining deals being done at five to six percent, and the living wage number ... you can see that the low point in wages looks like it's probably occurred in the December quarter. As the economy picks up through the course of 1997 and as the living wage rise
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"Even when the economy was slowing and the labour market was very sluggish in the latter part of 1996 there were still wage claims in annual terms around about 4.0 percent. It doesn't augur well for a really, really low inflation rate to justify another rate cut."
IVAN COLHOUN, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"It is obviously higher than expected. But the very low (quarterly) figure in August throws some question over that. At the time remember the Reserve Bank was very impressed with that. If you view August and November together then you are getting something more like a one percent per quarter average which is still not inconsistent with 2.5 pct inflation. But it just pulls into question whether wages have moderated or have simply plateaued at a pretty high level. I think it certainly would spotlight the Industrial Relations Commission and the "living wage claim. Our view (about monetary policy) is that on balance they (the RBA) are not going to move again unless the economy slows sharply.
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"This is the first time in the last nine quarters that the year-on-year female wage inflation rate has been higher than the male one. I think it's an anomoly and ... most of it reflects pay settlements in the health and education sectors. In general, in the public sector, the link between pay inflation and and price inflation is fairly tenuous. My guess would be, notwithstanding the intially adverse bond market reaction, that the Reserve Bank can probably discount this figure and that it shouldn't stand in the way of a further decline in interest rates."
GUY BRUTEN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, SBC WARBURG:

"They were a bit stronger than we thought. I think it keeps wages chugging along at four percent year on year which is still consistent with inflation at around two to 2.5 percent. Certainly it's not a downside surprise on inflation like we had through last year, but it's not a great shock on the upside. It doesn't change the inflation outlook in any way."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"My own feeling is that we are at 6.0 percent cash for quite a while to come. The data wasn't quite high enough to suggest there is a real problem out there. But it's really a critical issue where these wage claims come in now, particularly the safety net claim, which will determine how comfortable or not the Reserve Bank is with the wages environment."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
